chunks: Sahl ibn Ziyad from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Shammun from Abdullah ibn al-Rahman al-Asam from Mis'ma ibn al-Malik from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'From the edge of the well of Ma'tin to the edge of the well of Ma'tin is forty cubits, and from the edge of the well of Nadih to the edge of the well of Nadih is sixty cubits, and from the source of the spring to the source of the spring is five hundred cubits, and the road, when its people dispute over it, its boundary is seven cubits.'

key_terms.بِئْرِ النَّاضِحِ: The well of Nadih (watering place for animals)
key_terms.بِئْرِ الْمَعْطِنِ: The well of Ma'tin (a specific type of well or place name used in legal examples)

ai.seo_question: What are the legal boundaries for private water sources and roads in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this hadith provides the foundational metrics for *haram* (protected zones) in Shia jurisprudence, distinguishing between private water rights and communal road usage. The specific measurements—forty cubits for wells, sixty for watering spots, and five hundred for springs—reflect the practical needs of agrarian society in early Islamic Medina, ensuring that water sources remain accessible while preventing monopolization. This legal framework underscores the Shia emphasis on balancing individual property rights with the public good (*maslaha*), a principle deeply rooted in the Prophet’s teachings on resource management.
